notes.label: Present participle
notes.body: The present participle catches Aristodicus in the act, so the god's reaction is immediate.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.trans: a voice from the inner sanctuary
notes.body: A voice with no speaker comes from the shrine no visitor may enter, which makes the moment eerie and awe-inspiring.

notes.label: Direct speech
notes.body: For the first time the god speaks for himself, so the reader hears divine anger directly.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.body: The superlative with "of men" makes him the worst of all mankind, which turns his claim to be defending piety upside down.

notes.label: Rhetorical question
notes.body: An indignant question that needs no answer, which gives the voice a tone of outraged authority.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: "My suppliants" comes first, so the reader sees the god accepting the comparison Aristodicus has staged.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: κεραΐζω is used of sacking a city, which makes the removal of a few nests sound like an act of war against the god.

notes.label: Understatement (litotes)
notes.body: Aristodicus is not thrown by the god's fury, which shows he expected this reply and makes him seem confident to the point of arrogance.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The same respectful address that opened his question (line 94) now introduces an accusation, so the reader hears the irony.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The pronoun points the finger at the god, which makes Aristodicus sound like a speaker cross-examining a rival.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.quote: αὐτὸς μὲν ... βοηθεῖς, Κυμαίους δὲ κελεύεις ... ἐκδιδόναι
notes.trans: you yourself help ... but you order the Cymaeans to hand over
notes.body: The god's own conduct is set against his instructions to Cyme, so the reader sees the inconsistency Aristodicus wants to expose.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.body: The same noun in two different cases, which sharpens the comparison between the god's suppliants and Cyme's.

notes.label: Repetition
notes.trans: you order ... yes, I do order
notes.body: The god picks up Aristodicus' own verb, so the reader expects an apology and gets a reversal.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: The god admits the charge with a blunt "yes", which takes Aristodicus and the reader by surprise.

notes.label: Parallelism
notes.body: Two purpose clauses, one positive and one negative, reveal that the first answer was a deliberate test.

notes.label: Plural verbs
notes.trans: having acted impiously ... you may perish ... you may come
notes.body: The plurals spread the guilt to the whole city, so the reader sees that all of Cyme is on trial.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.body: The god threatens swift destruction for anyone who gives up a suppliant, which hangs over the rest of Pactyes' story.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The story ends on the oracle itself, the place the Cymaeans should never have come to with such a question.

questions: How does the god's reaction to the birds prove Aristodicus' point, and how does the god's final answer go beyond it?
What act of impiety does the god mean by ἀσεβήσαντες (line 112)? Who would commit it?
Was the god's first answer a lie? How might you defend it?
What should the Cymaeans have done when Pactyes arrived, according to this story? Do you agree?
How might this story be used in a modern debate about asylum?

context.body:
The Cymaeans found a way to avoid both handing Pactyes over and keeping him: they sent him away to Mytilene on Lesbos. When they heard that the Mytilenaeans were about to sell him to Mazares, they moved him again, to the island of Chios. There he took refuge as a suppliant in the temple of Athena, Guardian of the City.

It did not save him. The Chians dragged him out of the temple and gave him up to the Persians; their reward was Atarneus, a stretch of land on the mainland opposite Lesbos. Herodotus adds that for a long time afterwards no Chian would use barley grown at Atarneus in any offering to the gods: land bought at the price of a suppliant was polluted.

Set beside this story, the ending is pointed. The god at Branchidae had told the Cymaeans what happens to those who give up a suppliant, and the Chians did exactly that.
